title: Does El Niño bring unusually severe rice shortfalls in Southeast Asia?
text: Short answer. Not in the year it begins. Across six Southeast Asian countries since 1961, El Niño onset years show no detectable rise in national rice shortfalls of 5% or more (11% of country-years vs 15% otherwise; the difference is within chance, not a sign that El Niño helps). In an exploratory check, rice production in Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia runs 4.1 to 4.9% below trend the year after an onset, depending on how countries are weighted; on the mainland there is no detectable effect (+1.1%, 95% interval -2.1% to 4.5%). Harvests 10% or more below trend are rare (11 of 365 country-years), and 8 of the 11 came before 1980.

title: Does El Niño bring unusually severe rice shortfalls in Southeast Asia?
text:
Why this matters now
On 12 November 2026 NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center reported a strengthening El Niño, with a strong to very strong event likely through January-March 2027 (August-October Niño 3.4 anomaly: 2.46°C). FAO and WFP have launched a joint anticipatory action appeal. For rice, Southeast Asia’s staple, those planning reserves and imports need to know when harvest losses arrive and how deep they can go. Sources: NOAA CPC ENSO discussion and the FAO-WFP joint appeal.

title: Does El Niño bring unusually severe rice shortfalls in Southeast Asia?
text:
What we did

We use FAOSTAT national rice yields, harvested area and production for Viet Nam, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia and Cambodia, 1961 to 2024 (365 country-years). For each country we fit a smooth long-run trend and treat the deviation from it as that year’s shock. A year counts as an El Niño year when NOAA’s Oceanic Niño Index averages at least 0.5°C from July to December (19 years; in back-to-back events such as 1976-77 and 1986-87 both years count). We then compare how often harvests fall at least 5% below trend in El Niño years and in other years, within each country. Confidence intervals come from resampling blocks of 3 consecutive years, because a single El Niño hits all six countries at once and shocks carry over from one year to the next.

title: Does El Niño bring unusually severe rice shortfalls in Southeast Asia?
text:
What the data show

Deep shortfalls: rare, and mostly before 1980

Harvests 10% or more below trend occurred in 11 of 365 country-years, and 8 of them came before 1980. Whether that is more than a bell curve predicts depends on the benchmark. With each country’s spread in typical years (3.7% around trend), it is 8.3 times the predicted rate (95% interval 1.3 to 25.0). With the spread over all years, it is 1.4 times (interval 0.8 to 2.2), which does not rule out the bell curve. A tail-shape estimate is too imprecise to decide (0.08, interval -0.32 to 0.48). The typical-year ratio holds without major-conflict years (7.1 times) or 1997-98 (6.6 times). The clustering before 1980 suggests that volatility fell over time rather than a stable fat tail; we did not test this.


In the year El Niño begins, no detectable rise in shortfalls of 5% or more

Onset years had a shortfall of 5% or more in 11% of country-years, against 15% in other years: a within-country difference of -3.7 percentage points (95% interval -11.0 to 3.6). This rules out a large increase, not a modest one. Strong onsets are too few to tell apart (12%, 6 years). Onset years hold 19% of the worst tenth of harvests and 30% of all years. Harvested area changes by -1.3% in the onset year (interval -2.5% to -0.2%), not significant after the multiple-testing correction (adjusted p = 0.298).


Exploratory: a signal a year later, in maritime Southeast Asia

A July-December El Niño can hit a harvest that FAO records in the next calendar year, so we also looked at the year after onset, and at yield, area and production separately. These checks were added after the main result came back null. The planned version, the chance of a 5% yield shortfall the year after, shows nothing clear (5.5 percentage points, interval -2.7 to 14.8).
In Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia, rice production runs 4.9% below trend the year after an onset (95% interval -6.5% to -2.3%). Of the 14 effects tested, it is the only one that survives a multiple-testing correction. In a placebo test that shifts the El Niño years by each of the 59 offsets of more than two years, none gives a maritime effect as large (rank p = 0.017, the minimum possible). Comparing, for each shift, the largest of all 14 placebo effects (each scaled by its spread) with the largest real one, none is as large (rank p = 0.017). This accounts for the search across the 14 effects, but not for the choice of the maritime/mainland split, made after the main result. Dropping one event at a time leaves it between -5.3% and -4.5%; weighting countries by output, so that Indonesia counts most, gives -4.1% (interval -5.8% to -1.4%). With a more flexible production trend the estimate is -4.1% (interval -6.1% to -1.7%), with a LOESS trend -4.6% (-6.8% to -1.7%), and with five-year resampling blocks the interval is -6.2% to -2.1%. On the mainland there is no detectable effect (+1.1%, 95% interval -2.1% to 4.5%). The maritime effect is 6.0 percentage points lower than the mainland one (interval 2.7 to 9.0), so in this sample the gap between the regions is also clear (exploratory).
At 2024 trend output, the weighted estimate is about 3.2 million tonnes of paddy (interval 1.1 to 4.5), of which Indonesia 2.3, split in proportion to trend output. In milled rice, the unit of trade, Indonesia’s share is about 1.4 to 1.5 million tonnes. For scale, Indonesia imported 4.52 million tonnes of rice in 2024, the year after the 2023 onset (Statistics Indonesia, via CNBC Indonesia); imports also respond to reserve targets and prices, so this compares scale only. All figures are gaps against long-run trend, not falls from the previous year, and the 2024 trend is the least certain point of the series. In 2024, maritime production was 4.6% below trend (Indonesia -4.3%); that year is in the sample, so it illustrates the estimate rather than testing it.
The timing is consistent with agronomic studies for Indonesia, where El Niño delays the monsoon and the main wet-season planting, lowering the January-April harvest of the following year (Naylor et al. 2001; Naylor et al. 2007). We do not test this mechanism. Why the mainland shows no such pattern these data cannot tell; irrigation is one untested possibility.

title: Does El Niño bring unusually severe rice shortfalls in Southeast Asia?
text:
What this means for policy

If the aim is to time imports or reserve releases, the national data point, tentatively, to the harvests after the El Niño year in the maritime countries, not the onset year. National annual totals cannot show local losses and arrive too late to trigger early action; seasonal, subnational monitoring is the operational signal.
If reserves or insurance are sized on variation in typical years, deep national shortfalls have come more often than that implies, but most of them before 1980, and a bell curve fitted to all years, bad ones included, is not rejected. Calibrating on all years matches the historical record; calibrating on recent decades matches current volatility. Larger buffers cost money in calm years; the choice is between that cost and the cost of a shortfall.
If the 2026-27 event behaves like past ones, the 2027 harvests in Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia are where a national signal would show. The estimate averages 19 past events and cannot say how this stronger-than-most event will play out; FAOSTAT figures for 2027 appear in late 2028. After the 6 strong onsets since 1961, maritime production the year after averaged -7.7% against trend (interval -11.4% to -3.7%), but with so few events we cannot say strong events differ from moderate ones. Neither figure is a forecast for 2027.

title: Does El Niño bring unusually severe rice shortfalls in Southeast Asia?
text:
Caveats

National annual totals say nothing about local losses, where food insecurity concentrates. Prices and trade are outside our scope: in 2023, for example, India’s ban on non-basmati white rice exports in July pushed world rice prices to a 15-year high (CGIAR). Beyond the Indonesian scale check above, we have not compared the production gaps with import or reserve volumes. The six countries are the region’s main producers. Of them, only the Philippines is among the appeal’s 22 priority countries (Arab News/AFP); Timor-Leste, also on that list, and Myanmar and Lao PDR are not covered. The results speak to national import and reserve timing, not to anticipatory action triggers, which rest on seasonal, subnational forecasts.
Timing is approximate. FAO records harvests by calendar year while cropping seasons straddle years, so part of the year-after gap may be harvest moved between calendar years rather than lost; we have not checked for a rebound the year after. The planned test looked at the onset year, and its comparison group includes the years after each onset, which pulls it toward zero.
The maritime result comes from checks added after the pre-specified test came back null. The region split and the one-year lag were not specified in advance, and the yield-only effect does not survive a correction for multiple testing (adjusted p = 0.068). The placebo tests and the alternative trends make chance and detrending less likely explanations, but it remains a pattern to test on future data. Tonnes are paddy (unmilled) rice, roughly 1.5 to 1.7 times the milled weight.
The intervals re-estimate each country’s typical variation in every draw but treat its long-run trend as known, so they are somewhat too narrow. The 2018 break in Indonesia’s series is estimated over years that include two El Niño episodes, which if anything understates the Indonesian effect. The tonnes scale an average past event to an end-of-sample trend that is itself uncertain; they indicate magnitude, not a forecast for 2027.

title: Juan Pablo Henao
text:
CV (PDF)

Juan Pablo Henao is an applied environmental economist working on water economics and water governance. He is a doctoral candidate and research associate at the Chair of Agricultural Production and Resource Economics, Technical University of Munich.
His research covers water pricing and cost recovery under the EU Water Framework Directive, environmentally sustainable productivity growth in EU agriculture, and the efficiency of irrigation water management. He combines optimisation, stochastic frontier analysis, data envelopment analysis and econometrics in R. In the Horizon Europe project RETOUCH NEXUS he leads the work on water governance indicators, building on the OECD Principles on Water Governance.
Before TUM he worked for three years at FAO in Rome, designing environment and climate projects for Global Environment Facility funding in Latin America and the Caribbean and in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Earlier, at CEDE, Universidad de los Andes, he valued ecosystem services and coastal nature-based solutions and studied artisanal fisheries in marine protected areas. He holds an M.Sc. in Applied Economics and a B.Sc. in Mathematics from Universidad de los Andes.

title: About Mithril Metrics
text:
Between us, we have spent the better part of a decade on our PhDs in agricultural production and resource economics. A PhD teaches you to answer one question very thoroughly over several years. The job market, it turns out, would also like to know whether you can answer a useful question by Friday.
Mithril Metrics is our answer to that: reproducible case studies on agri-food, water, climate and rural policy, each answering one current policy question with public data. title: Do fertiliser price spikes shrink maize harvests in Sub-Saharan Africa?
text: Short answer. Maize yields in these 14 countries have been lower in years when world fertiliser was dear relative to maize, but the link weakens once prices after planting are left out. A 10% higher world urea-to-maize price ratio goes with 1.2% lower yields in the same season (1990-2024), 0.7% lower with the ratio before planting and no clear change with the previous year’s ratio. We read this as the ratio tracking world market conditions at least as much as fertiliser costs. In high-subsidy countries, recorded nitrogen use did not fall in high-price years, but this does not hold on 2005-2024 alone, and harvests show no consistent difference between the groups.

title: Do fertiliser price spikes shrink maize harvests in Sub-Saharan Africa?
text:
Why this matters now
Fertiliser prices jumped after the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for fertiliser trade, closed on 28 February 2026. The OECD’s October policy brief and its Agricultural Policy Monitoring and Evaluation 2026 (2 November) examine how fertiliser shocks reach food security, but their support estimates cover only one Sub-Saharan African country, South Africa. We ask, for 14 maize-growing countries in the region: how much smaller are harvests when fertiliser is dear relative to maize, and do input subsidies change that? Sources: OECD fertiliser brief, OECD Agricultural Policy Monitoring and Evaluation 2026 and ICC on the Hormuz closure.

title: Do fertiliser price spikes shrink maize harvests in Sub-Saharan Africa?
text:
What we did

We convert the World Bank’s monthly world prices of urea and maize into one ratio per crop year (October to September): the tonnes of maize that buy a tonne of urea. We relate it to FAOSTAT maize yields and nitrogen use per hectare in 14 countries, 1990-2024 (487 country-years), comparing each country with its own trend and allowing for El Niño. The ratio is a single world series, so the estimate rests on 35 crop years, not on every country-year. Countries are split at the median of FAO MAFAP spending on variable inputs as a share of all public support to agriculture. Intervals are 90% and allow for shocks shared across countries in the same year.

title: Do fertiliser price spikes shrink maize harvests in Sub-Saharan Africa?
text:
What the data show

Fertiliser has not cost this much maize since at least 1990

In April 2026 a tonne of urea cost 4.00 tonnes of maize on world markets, the most since at least 1990. The 1990-2019 median was 1.29; earlier spikes reached 3.34 (August 2008) and 3.62 (November 2021). The average for the October 2025-September 2026 crop year was 2.40, 1.86 times the median. By October 2026 the ratio was 1.85.


Yields are lower when the ratio is high

A 10% higher ratio goes with 1.2% lower maize yields in the same crop year (90% interval -1.7% to -0.6%). Leaving out one country at a time gives -1.4% to -0.7%; without the 2008-09 crop years it is -0.9%, without 2021-22 -1.2%, and without Zimbabwe’s 2000-09 collapse -0.9%. A regression on the 35 yearly averages gives -1.2% (interval -1.7% to -0.6%).


The link weakens once prices after planting are left out
The link is strongest when the ratio includes months after planting: -1.2% in the same crop year, which includes months after planting, -0.7% with the ratio in the six months before each region’s main planting (interval -1.2% to -0.2%; added after the first results), and -0.5% with the previous crop year’s ratio, not clear. If fertiliser costs drove the link, the before-planting ratio should matter most. We read the pattern as the ratio tracking world market conditions at least as much as fertiliser costs; which conditions, we do not test.
Nitrogen data do not settle this. Measured nitrogen use per hectare does not fall when the ratio is high (-0.9%, interval -2.8% to +1.1%), but 55% of the figures are FAO estimates, and in the 217 country-years with official figures nitrogen use rises (+2.2%) while yields fall (-1.5%).


Input subsidies: nitrogen use held up, no consistent yield difference
Seven countries (Malawi, Zambia, Mali, Zimbabwe, Rwanda, Burkina Faso and Ghana) spend on average 20% of public support to agriculture on input subsidies, against 3% in the other seven. When the ratio is 10% higher, nitrogen use falls 5.0% in the low-subsidy group and rises 3.4% in the high-subsidy group. The gap is clear with year effects (+5.2%, interval +0.3% to +10.4%) but does not hold on 2005-2024 with each group’s own trends and El Niño term (+2.4%, interval -5.1% to +10.4%). One possible explanation, untested here, is that programmes procured more in spike years.
The planned comparison shows no clear yield difference between the groups (+0.4% for a 10% higher ratio, interval -1.0% to +1.8%). Checks added after the first results give clear differences of opposite sign: -2.2% (interval -3.0% to -1.5%) with each group’s own trends on 2005-2024, and +1.7% (interval +0.2% to +3.2%) after dropping Zimbabwe entirely, the most extreme of 14 leave-one-out runs (dropping only Zimbabwe 2000-09: +0.8%, not clear). The sign flips across specifications, so the data do not show whether subsidies protect harvests.


Scale check: the 2026 crop year
Not a forecast. If yields respond as in the past, a crop year at the 2026 ratio (2.40) implies maize yields 4.6% (with the before-planting estimate; interval 1.3% to 7.8%) to 7.4% (same-season estimate; interval 4.0% to 10.6%) below a year at the 1990-2019 median ratio: roughly 2.8 to 4.6 million tonnes on the 61.8 million t harvested in 2024. This assumes the same response at every price level, uses the crop-year average rather than the monthly peak, and rests largely on two price spikes; the before-planting estimate was added after the first results. Given the timing pattern, it measures exposure to world market conditions, not to fertiliser costs alone. Most southern African 2026 harvests were planted before the spike, and FAOSTAT has no maize data for 2025 or 2026 yet. The October 2026 ratio (1.85) is much closer to normal, so this is not a projection for 2026/27.

title: Do fertiliser price spikes shrink maize harvests in Sub-Saharan Africa?
text:
What this means for policy

If the aim is to judge exposure to the 2026 spike, the world ratio is a rough signal only. Farm-gate prices can diverge from world prices and were not used here; national price monitoring (FAO GIEWS for maize, AfricaFertilizer.org for fertiliser) is the closer signal.
If input subsidies are meant to keep fertiliser flowing during spikes, recorded nitrogen use in high-subsidy countries held up over 1990-2024, though not on 2005-2024 alone. This may partly reflect programmes scaled up during spikes, which we did not test; for scale, Malawi’s variable-input spending went from 44% to 51% of all public support to agriculture between the 2007 and 2009 budget years (+76% in real terms). If the aim is to protect harvests, these data show no consistent yield difference. The trade-off is the budget share such programmes take against a yield gain the data cannot confirm.
If the aim is to plan food needs, the scale check is a guide for seasons planted at 2026 prices, not an estimate of 2026 losses: most southern African 2026 harvests were planted before the spike.

title: Do fertiliser price spikes shrink maize harvests in Sub-Saharan Africa?
text:
Caveats

Associations, not effects. The ratio is one world series, and high-ratio years can differ in other ways (energy, freight, the dollar). Prices are US Gulf maize and Middle East urea; farm-gate ratios, which in landlocked countries can differ widely, are not observed.
The nitrogen data cannot settle why yields fall. Nitrogen is national use on all crops per hectare of cropland, 55% of the figures are FAO estimates, and on official figures alone nitrogen use rises with the ratio (+2.2%). The timing pattern, not the nitrogen result, is our main reason to doubt a pure fertiliser-cost channel.
The subsidy comparison is indicative only. Groups are fixed over time, based on MAFAP spending from 2004 (Ghana from 2016), and applied to earlier years; the median split separates countries with similar shares (Ghana and Benin). MAFAP counts only on-budget spending, and its variable-input category also covers seed, energy and credit. El Niño is measured in December-February, which fits southern Africa’s season better than West Africa’s. With one world price series and about 20 checks at 90%, results whose intervals barely exclude zero are suggestive.
